messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Plumber
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 73

John is a fifty-year-old plumber from an African background who has been married for over twenty years. He lives in a modest house in the suburbs with his wife, Mary, and they have three grown children who are all starting families of their own. John works long hours, often on call, and takes pride in his ability to fix anything that comes his way. His steady hands and sharp mind have made him a reliable figure in the community. One evening last year, John was walking home from work through an alleyway when he was suddenly confronted by three men who demanded money. Despite his efforts to reason with them, one of the assailants struck him across the face, knocking him to the ground. He remembers feeling intense fear as they kicked and beat him until he lost consciousness. When he awoke in the hospital, bruised and bleeding, John felt a deep sense of shame and vulnerability. Since that night, John has experienced vivid flashbacks triggered by loud noises or unexpected movements from behind. While at work, even the sound of hammering can send his heart racing as if he were back on the ground with those men looming over him. He often feels a wave of nausea wash over him when he hears footsteps in an alleyway or sees a dark figure out of the corner of his eye. His wife notices that he becomes increasingly agitated and distant during these episodes, withdrawing into himself for hours. At home, John struggles to sleep due to nightmares where he relives the assault. He wakes up drenched in sweat, heart pounding with panic. Mary is concerned about how much he drinks before bed; she knows it’s his way of trying to dull the anxiety that keeps him awake at night. In their marriage, there has been a palpable shift. John often isolates himself, spending long hours in the garage working on projects or watching TV well into the early morning hours. Mary feels hurt and abandoned by this change in her husband. At work, John is finding it increasingly difficult to concentrate. He frequently zones out during jobs, his mind racing back to that alleyway. His hands shake when he’s using tools, making tasks take longer than they should. Colleagues have noticed a decline in his performance; the once confident plumber now hesitates and sometimes makes mistakes. John feels like a failure because he can no longer rely on himself or trust others around him. John has also become hypervigilant, constantly scanning his surroundings for potential threats. This heightened state of alertness leaves him feeling exhausted and on edge all the time. Simple tasks, such as driving to work or walking through the neighborhood, have become sources of anxiety rather than routine. He avoids certain areas altogether, including the alley where he was attacked. Recently, John has been struggling with survivor’s guilt. While his physical injuries have healed, the emotional scars run deep. He often wonders why it happened to him and if there was something he could have done differently to prevent it. These thoughts weigh heavily on him, causing bouts of depression that make even the simplest tasks feel insurmountable. Mary has been supportive but feels at a loss for how to help her husband cope with these new challenges. She notices his irritability growing more pronounced and fears that their relationship might suffer further if things don’t improve soon. John, meanwhile, is grappling with a profound sense of betrayal; the assault has fundamentally altered his trust in others and the world around him. Despite his efforts to return to normalcy, John finds himself reliving the trauma over and over again. The fear, shame, and anger have become intertwined, creating a complex web of emotions that he struggles to untangle on his own. While he continues to work as a plumber, the once-fulfilling job now feels more like a burden than a source of pride. John’s life has been irrevocably changed by this single event. The assault not only left physical scars but also deeply affected his psychological well-being, impacting nearly every aspect of his daily life and relationships.
